title: Pregnancy and postpartum stroke
summary: Pregnancy should not delay stroke evaluation or treatment: image without delay (CT with or without contrast, and MRI without contrast, are considered safe), and IVT and EVT are supported when benefits outweigh risks (AHA 2026 maternal statement). Severe hypertension (≥160/110 confirmed within 15 minutes) is an emergency; magnesium and antihypertensives are the cornerstones for preeclampsia and eclampsia. Consider ICH, SAH, CVT, RCVS and PRES as well as ischemic stroke, especially postpartum.
consider: Establish the pregnancy or postpartum stage, blood pressure and likely mechanism.
Involve vascular neurology and maternal-fetal medicine early; a transradial approach is preferred for endovascular procedures when possible.
Plan for infant care, breastfeeding and rehabilitation support.
caution: Acute stroke is not by itself an indication for delivery, and the statement supplies no universal antithrombotic choice.

title: Stroke with active cancer
summary: Complete the usual arterial and cardiac workup before blaming active cancer: it can coexist with conventional mechanisms or cause thrombosis directly. The 2026 AHA statement grades the certainty of cancer-related causation and highlights how uncertain treatment remains.
consider: Has the usual arterial and cardiac evaluation been completed rather than attributing the event to cancer alone?
What clinical evidence supports cancer-related thrombosis or another cancer-associated mechanism?
Have recurrent thrombosis, bleeding, cancer treatment and patient goals been reviewed together?
caution: A cancer diagnosis does not establish the mechanism or an automatic anticoagulant indication.

title: Stroke with prior disability or dementia
summary: Prior disability or dementia was usually excluded from reperfusion trials, but observational data show many patients can return to their own baseline. AHA 2026: within 6 h with ASPECTS ≥6, EVT is reasonable at prestroke mRS 2 (2a) and might be reasonable at mRS 3–4 (2b). Decide with the actual baseline, supports and the outcomes the patient values.
consider: What were the patient’s actual baseline function, supports and valued activities?
What additional disability might this stroke cause, and what outcome would the patient consider worthwhile?
Are treatment risks and the limits of the evidence being discussed without relying on a baseline score alone?
caution: Prior disability alone does not decide treatment, and observational benefit does not apply to every patient.

title: Perioperative stroke
summary: Before noncardiac, nonneurological surgery, include recent stroke, vascular disease and the procedure in the risk discussion and plan antithrombotic changes as a team; after surgery, any new deficit should trigger the stroke pathway with prompt imaging (AHA statement).
consider: Are recent stroke history, vascular disease and the proposed procedure included in the risk discussion?
Are perioperative medication changes and the responsible teams clearly documented?
Does a new postoperative deficit trigger the local stroke pathway with prompt imaging?
caution: Surgery timing after a recent stroke and perioperative medication changes need procedure-specific multidisciplinary review.

title: Sex, gender and equitable stroke care
summary: Base reperfusion decisions on the individual's findings and priorities; population-level sex and gender differences in recognition, access and endovascular outcomes do not create separate eligibility rules. Much of the evidence records sex rather than gender, leaving gaps (AHA statement).
consider: Could differences in recognition, access, baseline circumstances or support be influencing care?
Are decisions based on the individual’s clinical findings and priorities?
Does the cited evidence actually address this patient population?
caution: Population-level differences do not establish an individual treatment effect or a separate eligibility rule.

title: Stroke in neonates and children
summary: Suspect stroke in any child with a sudden focal deficit, including a first seizure (AHA 2026, COR 1). Image with MRI/MRA, or CT/CTA if MRI is not available within 25 minutes (2a). Alteplase may be considered from 28 days to 18 years within 4.5 h for a disabling deficit (2b). EVT by experienced neurointerventionalists can be effective for LVO in children aged 6 or older within 24 h (2a) and may be reasonable from 28 days to 6 years (2b).

recommendations.text: In pediatric patients with sudden-onset focal neurological deficits, including first-time seizure, acute stroke is recommended to be suspected to enable timely diagnosis.

In pediatric patients aged 28 days to 18 years with confirmed AIS presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset with disabling deficits, IVT with alteplase may be considered as it appears safe, though efficacy is uncertain.

In pediatric patients 6 years or older with acute neurological symptoms from ischemic stroke due to LVO within 6 hours of symptom onset, EVT performed by experienced neurointerventionalists can be effective to improve functional outcomes.

consider: Call pediatric stroke expertise early and use age-appropriate imaging.
Consider age-specific mechanisms and mimics.
Follow-up should cover development, learning, family support and recurrence prevention.
caution: Adult pathways cannot simply be transferred to neonates or children.

title: Sickle cell cerebrovascular disease
summary: New neurological symptoms in sickle cell disease need urgent stroke and hematology assessment together. Eligible adults can receive IVT without excess sICH or other thrombolytic complications (AHA 2026, 2a). ASH guidance covers overt stroke, silent cerebral injury and prevention; transfusion and disease-modifying decisions belong with the treating specialists.
consider: Are the sickle cell genotype, prior cerebral events and preventive treatment history known?
Has a new neurologic event prompted urgent stroke and hematology assessment?
Is the age- and disease-specific screening and follow-up plan clear?
caution: An adult atherosclerotic-stroke pathway does not cover sickle cell disease.

title: Dysphagia, nutrition and oral care
summary: Screen swallowing at the bedside before any oral intake (AHA 2026, COR 1); if the screen fails or cannot be done, an instrumental assessment (FEES or videofluoroscopy) is reasonable (2a). Start enteral feeding within 7 days (COR 1): nasogastric tube first, and gastrostomy if unsafe swallowing is expected beyond 2–3 weeks (2a). An oral hygiene protocol may reduce pneumonia (2b).
consider: Is the current intake plan clear to everyone, including medication routes?
Does a concerning screen or clinical change need specialist assessment?
Are hydration, oral care and reassessment in the plan?
caution: A screening result is not the full swallowing diagnosis; in FOOD, PEG led to more death or poor outcome than nasogastric feeding.

title: Stroke-associated pneumonia
summary: Diagnose stroke-associated pneumonia clinically, not from a risk score. Prevent it with swallow screening, oral care, positioning and mobility; do not give prophylactic antibiotics (AHA 2026, COR 3; ESO 2026). Treat confirmed pneumonia according to local microbiology.
consider: Is pneumonia supported by a clinical assessment rather than a risk score alone?
Have swallowing, positioning, mobility and nutritional needs been reviewed?
If pneumonia is diagnosed, is treatment aligned with local microbiology and antimicrobial guidance?
caution: Most ESO recommendations rest on expert consensus because direct evidence is limited.

title: Stroke-unit nursing and daily care
summary: Care for all ages in an organized stroke unit with a trained interdisciplinary team and standardized orders (AHA 2026, COR 1). Nurse-initiated fever, glucose and swallowing protocols reduced death or dependency (QASC: 42 vs 58%). Make phase-specific monitoring and escalation explicit and carry unresolved issues into discharge planning.
consider: Are phase-specific monitoring and escalation responsibilities clear?
Have functional needs, safety concerns and family teaching been incorporated into daily care?
Are unresolved inpatient issues carried forward into the discharge plan?
caution: These statements do not set a universal monitoring frequency or replace response to deterioration.

title: Systemic complications during stroke admission
summary: Watch for infection, cardiac events, hyperglycemia, fever and delirium. Keep persistent hyperglycemia at 140–180 mg/dL rather than 80–130 (SHINE: no benefit, severe hypoglycemia 2.6%), treat fever to normothermia, and avoid routine bladder catheters (AHA 2026, COR 3: Harm). Aphasia, delirium and neurological worsening can coexist.
consider: Have new systemic symptoms or laboratory changes been assessed alongside the neurological course?
Could aphasia be limiting the examination, and does fluctuating attention need broader reassessment?
Do medical, nursing and rehabilitation teams share a complication plan?
caution: A bedside impression cannot exclude an acute cause of change.

title: VTE prevention after stroke
summary: Immobile after ischemic stroke: intermittent pneumatic compression from admission (AHA 2026, COR 1; CLOTS 3 proximal DVT 8.5 vs 12.1%), and prophylactic-dose heparin (UFH or LMWH) is reasonable (2a). Do not use elastic compression stockings (COR 3: Harm). After ICH, start IPC on the day of diagnosis (AHA 2022, COR 1).
consider: What are the current mobility, VTE and bleeding risks?
Is IPC fitted and worn as intended, with skin checks?
Before heparin prophylaxis, review renal function, recent treatment and hemorrhage risk.
caution: Graduated compression stockings are not equivalent to intermittent pneumatic compression.

title: Spasticity and contracture prevention
summary: Recognize poststroke spasticity early — pain, hygiene, positioning or care tasks affected by tone — and refer for rehabilitation assessment before contracture and secondary impairment set in (AHA 2026 statement).
consider: Are pain, hygiene, positioning, mobility or care tasks affected by tone or restricted movement?
What active and passive functional goals matter to the patient and caregiver?
Is timely specialist or rehabilitation assessment needed?
caution: Increased tone is not the only cause of impaired movement; treatment follows a functional assessment.

title: Aphasia and communication rehabilitation
summary: Offer individualized speech-language therapy aimed at the communication activities that matter to the patient; digital and group formats can be considered within an appropriate rehabilitation plan (ESO 2025).
consider: Which communication activities matter most to the patient?
Are assessment and shared decisions adapted to language impairment?
Is the therapy plan feasible, sufficiently supported and reassessed as needs change?
caution: Aphasia does not establish impaired decision-making capacity, and evidence certainty differs across therapy comparisons.

title: Visual impairment and neglect
summary: Screen for visual problems — central vision, eye movements, visual fields, neglect and perception — because they are otherwise missed, and arrange specialist assessment and adaptations for reading and mobility (ESO 2025).
consider: Has the patient been assessed for the relevant type of visual impairment?
Do reading, mobility or daily activities require adaptations and specialist input?
Are visual findings communicated to the rehabilitation and follow-up teams?
caution: Different visual syndromes need different assessments, and this card does not establish driving fitness.

title: Motor recovery, walking and daily activity
summary: Link practice to tasks the patient needs in daily life and measure movement and participation goals over time. ESO 2025 covers upper-limb practice, gait training, transfer of therapy into daily life, group therapy and sit-to-stand training, with recommendations that differ in strength and population.
consider: Which movement and participation goals are being measured over time?
Is practice linked to tasks the patient needs in daily life?
Do cardiovascular stability, endurance and access support the proposed training approach?
caution: Results from chronic, stable stroke do not automatically apply during acute illness; dose needs a rehabilitation assessment.

title: Mood, anxiety, fatigue and psychosocial recovery
summary: Screen for depression with a structured inventory (AHA 2026, COR 1) and treat it with antidepressants and/or psychotherapy or other nonpharmacological options (COR 1). Ask about anxiety, fatigue and stress, and give patients and families education and access to interdisciplinary support.
consider: Which emotional symptoms or fatigue are limiting recovery or daily life?
Is a concerning screen followed by clinical assessment and a practical care pathway?
Do the patient and family have support, education and access to needed services?
caution: A screening score is not a diagnosis, and fatigue or distress should not be assigned a single cause without assessment.

title: Driving, seizures and return to participation
summary: Discuss driving and return to work explicitly at follow-up. Licensing after seizures is individualized and depends on medication effects, recurrence risk, local rules and access to alternative transport (AAN 2025 position statement).
consider: Are seizures, cognition, vision, motor function or medication effects relevant to the intended activity?
Have the applicable licensing rules and any specialist assessment requirements been checked?
What transport, workplace or rehabilitation support is needed?
caution: A position statement is not state law, a universal waiting period or individual clearance.

title: Long-term follow-up and primary care
summary: At every follow-up, reconcile risk-factor treatment and medications across clinicians, and rescreen cognition, mood, falls and unmet needs — they remain relevant beyond early recovery (AHA primary-care statement).
consider: Are risk-factor treatment and the medication list reconciled across clinicians?
Have changes in function, falls, cognition or mood prompted reassessment?
Are patient and caregiver priorities linked to referrals and a named follow-up plan?
caution: Prevention and rehabilitation plans need reassessment as health, function and support change.

title: Cognition after stroke and vascular brain injury
summary: Screen cognition after stroke against the person's baseline; vascular injury and preexisting neurodegeneration can interact, so look for associated conditions and plan safety, supports and follow-up across disciplines (AHA 2023). Impairment affects independence, employment and relationships.
consider: What has changed from the person’s cognitive and functional baseline?
Are language, mood, sensory limitations or acute illness affecting assessment?
Does the care plan address everyday safety, supports and follow-up evaluation?
caution: A single screen does not identify the cause or establish permanent impairment.

title: Sleep disorders and brain health
summary: Ask about sleep and screen for sleep-disordered breathing and insomnia, then confirm with diagnostic testing rather than assuming a diagnosis. Disturbed sleep is linked with worse cerebrovascular and cognitive outcomes, but treatment effects on those outcomes are not established (AHA 2024).
consider: Are sleep-disordered breathing, insomnia or other sleep symptoms affecting recovery?
Does screening warrant diagnostic evaluation rather than an assumed diagnosis?
Are sleep symptoms and treatment feasibility included in follow-up?
caution: A screening questionnaire does not diagnose sleep apnea, and association does not prove that treatment prevents stroke or dementia.

title: Brain health across the life span
summary: Address the vascular, sleep, mental-health and social factors relevant to the person's goals without overinterpreting observational findings; the 2026 AHA framework separates established knowledge from research questions.
consider: Which vascular, sleep, mental-health or social factors are relevant to this person’s goals?
Are potentially modifiable exposures and barriers discussed without overinterpreting observational findings?
Does the proposed intervention have evidence for the outcome being claimed?
caution: This framework is not a validated brain-health score or proof that any supplement, biomarker or lifestyle change prevents dementia.

title: Antiamyloid therapy and cerebrovascular risk
summary: Ask stroke patients about antiamyloid immunotherapy: it can cause amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (edema and hemorrhage), and acute antithrombotic and reperfusion decisions in treated patients need the current drug label and specialist input (AHA advisory).
consider: Is current or recent antiamyloid treatment known and communicated to the stroke team?
Could the presentation and imaging reflect ARIA, ischemia or another process?
Have the current drug label, imaging history and relevant specialists been consulted?
caution: This card gives no blanket antithrombotic or reperfusion permission; check the current drug label and stroke guidance.

title: In-hospital stroke recognition and response
summary: Every unit should be able to activate the stroke team immediately; use an organized protocol for emergent evaluation of acute deficits at any age (AHA 2026, COR 1). Hand over time last known well, the examination, imaging and recent procedures, and track delays for quality review.
consider: Can staff immediately activate the stroke response from this location?
Are timing, examination, imaging and relevant recent procedures communicated to the response team?
Are transfer barriers and delays captured for review?
caution: Being in a monitored setting does not ensure timely recognition.

title: Rural care, telestroke and transfer networks
summary: Without in-house stroke expertise, use telestroke for IVT decisions (AHA 2026, COR 1) and teleradiology for rapid image review (COR 1); EMS should go to the closest stroke-capable hospital, and direct transport to a thrombectomy center is reasonable where local access exists (2a). Agree transfer protocols that minimize door-in-door-out time (COR 1).
consider: What imaging, specialist and treatment capabilities are available at the referring and receiving sites?
Are clinical information, images and the transfer plan shared through a reliable process?
Is responsibility clear if connection, transport or destination capacity changes?
caution: Technology and center labels do not establish current local capability.

title: Transitions, discharge communication and continuity
summary: Before discharge, confirm that the patient's priorities, medication plan, open questions and the named follow-up owner reach the next setting, and that patient and care partner have usable information and a way to get help (AHA transitions statement).
consider: Are the patient’s priorities and support needs reflected in the next setting of care?
Are medication plans, outstanding questions and responsibility for follow-up clearly communicated?
Have the patient and care partner received usable information and a way to seek help?
caution: A completed discharge document does not establish a successful transition.

title: Rehabilitation access and recovery barriers
summary: Match the rehabilitation plan to documented functional needs and check coverage, travel and caregiving barriers early; name who will resolve barriers and reassess if access is delayed (AHA statements).
consider: Do coverage, travel, caregiving or other circumstances limit the proposed rehabilitation plan?
Are the recommended setting and services linked to documented functional needs?
Who will help resolve barriers and reassess needs if access is delayed?
caution: Placement availability is not the same as clinical suitability.

Are processes and outcomes measured with clear responsibility for improvement?
Are acute and postacute teams using shared expectations for coordinated care?
